tytul: Spiced pear pickles with cloves and cinnamon (NCHFP)
wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for pear pickles: peeled pickling pears simmered in a vinegar and sugar syrup with cinnamon, cloves and allspice, hot packed and processed in a boiling-water bath.

akapity: The recipe uses Seckel pears or other pickling pears; halve or quarter large pears.
NCHFP calls Asian pears borderline in acidity and gives them a separate acidifying procedure; this recipe does not name them, so this card does not cover Asian pears (nashi).
Besides cloves and cinnamon, the recipe also contains allspice.

sekcje.naglowek: Why you must not change the recipe
akapity: The whole product must contain a minimum, uniform level of acid so that botulism bacteria cannot grow.
Do not change the proportions of vinegar, fruit and water and do not use vinegar of unknown acidity; use only recipes with tested proportions.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): do not change the amounts of vinegar, water or pears and do not add other vegetables; the recipe is tested only in the proportions given.
White distilled vinegar and cider vinegar of 5% acidity are recommended for pickles.
Penn State Extension advises vinegar of 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and advises against diluting vinegar with water unless a research-tested recipe says so.

JarAtlas rule (cautious, for readers outside the USA): use the white distilled (spirit) vinegar the recipe lists, labelled 5% or 6% acidity; do not use 10% vinegar and do not dilute it with water to make 5% vinegar; add only the water the recipe lists.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.

For about 7 or 8 pint jars NCHFP lists 8 cups (2 quarts) of sugar, 4 cups (1 quart) of white vinegar (5%), 2 cups (1 pint) of water and 8 pounds (about 3.6 kg; 4 to 5 quarts) of Seckel or other pickling pears.
Spices: 8 cinnamon sticks in pieces 2 inches (about 5.1 cm) long, 2 tablespoons of whole cloves and 2 tablespoons of whole allspice.
Combine the sugar, vinegar, water and cinnamon sticks, and add the cloves and allspice tied in a clean, thin, white cloth.
Bring to a boil and simmer, covered, for about 30 minutes.
Wash the pears, remove the skins and all of the blossom end; you may leave the stems on.
Halve or quarter large pears.
To keep peeled pears from darkening, put them right after peeling into a cold solution of 1/2 teaspoon of ascorbic acid per 2 quarts (about 1.9 l) of water.
Drain them just before using.
Add the drained pears to the hot syrup, bring to a boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for another 20 to 25 minutes.
Pack the hot pears into hot pint jars and add to each jar one piece of cinnamon stick 2 inches (about 5.1 cm) long.
Cover the pears with boiling syrup, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace; the syrup must cover the pears.
Remove air bubbles and adjust the headspace if needed.
Wipe the rims with a damp clean paper towel, put on two-piece metal canning lids and process.
At 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) process pint jars in a boiling-water bath for 20 minutes.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–3000 ft (above 300 m up to 900 m) process them for 25 minutes.
At 3001–6000 ft (above 900 m up to 1800 m) process them for 30 minutes.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process them for 35 minutes.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m, 3000 ft becomes 900 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
The NCHFP table gives times only for pint jars.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): a pint holds about 473 ml, so a 0.5 l jar has no tested time in this recipe; use jars of up to 473 ml.
When you take the hot jars out of the canner, do not retighten the lids or bands; this can cut through the gasket and cause seal failures.

Cool the jars at room temperature for 12 to 24 hours, then remove only the screw bands (the metal rings of two-piece lids), leaving the flat lids on the jars, and test the seal: press the middle of the lid, and if it springs up when you release it, the jar is not sealed.

NCHFP calls Mason-type canning jars with self-sealing two-piece lids (a flat lid and a screw band) the best choice, and this seal test and the method on this card assume them; NCHFP does not recommend other commercial jars whose mouths cannot be sealed with two-piece canning lids for canning any food at home.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): use this card only with jars that take two-piece canning lids; it gives no method for twist-off jars or jars with glass lids, so do not use them for this recipe.
A sealed lid is concave, curved down slightly in the centre; if the centre is flat or bulging, the jar may not be sealed.
If a jar has not sealed at this check, keep it in the refrigerator and eat it within several days.

Store sealed jars in a clean, cool, dark, dry place, not above 95 °F (35 °C) and not near hot pipes, a stove or a furnace, in an uninsulated attic or in direct sunlight; in such conditions the food may spoil.
Before using a stored jar, check that the lid is tight and holds a vacuum: a good seal has a concave centre.
Look for streaks of dried food running from the top of the jar, rising air bubbles and unnatural colour.
When opening the jar, check for an unnatural smell, spurting liquid and cotton-like mould on the food or under the lid.
Do not taste food from a jar with an unsealed lid or with signs of spoilage.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw out such a jar.
